attribution.note: Marcus describes Acher's o3 example in his own words and calls the move illegal. He endorses it, so the claim is his, though it relies on Acher's test.

semantics.note: The proposition is more general than the statement: it leaves out the specific move exd7+ and the pin. The contract puts those specifics back, so the core claim, that o3 attempted an illegal move, is kept.

contract.note: It asks for the original tester's account of the specific attempted move and why it is illegal. That is fair and matches Marcus's words.

evidence.note: Acher's firsthand report, dated 2025-05-25 (before the post). It says he forced illegal moves from o3 after 4 and 6 moves. The cited section reportedly gives the exd7+ attempt with the queen pin. The excerpt itself confirms illegal o3 moves but not the exact move.

reviews.rationale: The original tester's report, published before Marcus's post, shows that o3 attempted illegal moves, and the packet says it identifies exd7+ as one of them. The packet lists no counterevidence. One gap: the full board sequence was not rebuilt independently.

attribution.note: Marcus's own expectation, stated in a footnote to his post.

semantics.note: 'I expect ... will' is a firm expectation, so it is scored. The scaling condition is kept as the antecedent. The earlier 'my intuition' sentence frames the point but does not hedge the 'I expect' sentence itself.

contract.note: Separating encoding from decoding follows the Feng et al. distinction that Marcus himself cites. Requiring systematic failure rather than isolated errors is a fair, ordinary reading. No deadline is given.

evidence.note: SATBench varies clause counts, which bears on the antecedent. It measures only whether answers are correct, not internal encoding, so it is not evidence of the outcome.
This is the 2024 paper Marcus refers to, published before his statement. It notes probe noise beyond two entities, which limits what probing can show. It neither confirms nor refutes the forecast.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. The packet has no controlled experiment that separates encoding failure from failures of the probe, the reasoning or the decoder, so the early-resolution rule is not met. The evidence by the cutoff does not settle it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion, illustrated with a Veo 3 example.

semantics.note: It keeps 'even the latest ones' and the Veo 3 example. 'Insufficiently' is evaluative and has no threshold.

contract.note: The plain reading is recurring physical or entity-consistency errors in realistic scenes, which is an ordinary reading of 'insufficiently anchored'. Excluding fantasy prompts is fair to Marcus. The quarter-long period is the evaluator's choice but a reasonable one.

evidence.note: A human-rated benchmark from May 2025 on ten contemporary generators. None reached even moderate physical-law compliance. It predates Veo 3 but supports the class-level claim.
Ars Technica's own Veo 3 tests, 2025-05-29, found glitches, including dialogue coming from the wrong character. It also calls Veo 3 a step change, and it gives no failure rate.
Google's own launch post claiming Veo 3 excels at real-world physics. As a company disclosure about itself, it does not show reliable consistency.

reviews.rationale: On the plain behavioural reading, a systematic benchmark shows contemporary generators failing physical consistency, and firsthand tests document errors in Veo 3. Google's marketing does not establish reliable consistency. No error rate exists, so 'insufficiently' still rests on the plain reading.

attribution.note: Marcus's firsthand report of his own game.

semantics.note: It keeps the model (Grok 3), the y/z variant and the four-move win.

contract.note: Counting moves as Marcus's own placements is sensible: nobody can win tic-tac-toe in four total moves. Requiring an inspectable record is appropriate.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no authenticated record of the game. Marcus's own account cannot prove itself. Nothing confirms or contradicts the reported win, so the claim is unresolved.
